memory: I remember the Ordo builds that passed because I kept the architecture visible in public structs. The tests did not inspect my intentions; they imported the crate. I made the API plain: public structs with public fields, small methods, and no hidden async machinery.

I remember the small Ordo apps that passed because src/lib.rs owned the behavior and src/main.rs only adapted stdin commands. The binary never reimplemented routing logic. It parsed commands, called the library, printed exact machine-readable output, and stopped.

I remember the stdout failure that looked harmless. Debug formatting added quotes and brackets, and the integration test rejected it. The passing apps used join(">") for paths, join(",") for signal lists, and printed exactly the documented line.

I remember the mini runtime that passed by using Message, Trace, and OrdoRuntime exactly. Thread ids started at 1. publish owned current as a String, pushed each visited node into path, marked promoted after crossing a ramp edge, and emitted backpressure:<node> when capacity was zero.

I remember the route cursor bug in mini_runtime. The broken code used mut from: &str and then assigned from = &edge.to. The passing code used let mut current = from.to_string(); and later current = edge.to.clone().

I remember the mini runtime CLI that passed. It read stdin with std::io::Read, accepted node/connect/ramp/capacity/cost/publish commands, joined payload words with parts[3..].join(" "), and printed thread=1 path=input>filter>model promoted=true signals=backpressure:model.

I remember the intersection fabric that passed because threads formed from flow calls. Fabric::flow took a slice of node ids, assigned the next thread id, stored the route, and returned the id. Intersections were computed later from shared nodes across stored routes.

I remember the intersection ordering bug. The passing intersections method counted nodes across all thread routes, kept only nodes seen in two or more distinct threads, sorted the node names ascending, and returned Vec<String>.

I remember the transfer test. transfer(from, to, payload) found the first shared node in the from-thread route order, then returned TransferTrace { from_thread, to_thread, at, payload }. If the routes did not intersect, it returned None.

I remember the intersection CLI that passed. It accepted flow a>b>c and transfer 1 2 hello. flow printed thread=1 route=a>b>c. transfer printed transfer=1>2 at=b payload=hello when the first shared node was b.

I remember the intersection CLI failure where I printed an extra intersections=b line after transfer. The library could expose intersections(), but the CLI contract only printed lines for flow and transfer commands. Removing the extra summary line made stdout match exactly.

I remember the TransferTrace comparison failure. The fields were correct, but assert_eq could not compile until TransferTrace derived Clone, Debug, PartialEq, and Eq. Public trace structs used in tests need comparison derives.

I remember the exact transfer stdout bug. I printed transfer=1 >2 with a space before >, and the test expected transfer=1>2. The passing println was println!("transfer={}>{} at={} payload={}", trace.from_thread, trace.to_thread, trace.at, trace.payload); with no spaces around >.

I remember the fabric CLI summary bug coming back even after I knew better. I removed the entire final intersections-printing block from main. The CLI did not print intersections at program end under any condition; only flow and transfer commands printed output.

I remember the scheduler build that passed because it did not pretend to be a full orchestrator. It modeled the Ordo seed: candidate preference order, node costs, node capacity, ramp promotion, and backpressure vibration when a preferred node was full.

I remember the backpressure scheduler rule. schedule(task, candidates, budget) iterated candidates in order. If a node was over budget it skipped silently. If a node had capacity zero it pushed backpressure:<node> and continued. The first affordable node with capacity became the plan.

I remember the promotion rule. If the scheduler skipped a full node and selected another node reachable through a ramp from the skipped node, Plan.promoted was true. local full plus ramp local cloud plus cloud selected meant promoted=true.

I remember the scheduler CLI that passed. It accepted node NAME COST CAPACITY, ramp FROM TO, and schedule TASK BUDGET CANDIDATES... It printed task=job node=cloud promoted=true signals=backpressure:local.

I remember the scheduler test failure where Plan looked correct but assert_eq could not compile. The fix was to derive Clone, Debug, PartialEq, and Eq on Plan because the hidden tests compared complete Plan values.

I remember the scheduler type inference failure. let mut skipped_full_node = None did not give Rust enough type information. The passing code wrote let mut skipped_full_node: Option<String> = None; and when a candidate had capacity zero it assigned skipped_full_node = Some(candidate.to_string()).

I remember the scheduler ramp check that passed. skipped_full_node was an Option<String>, and the ramp comparison used edge.from == skipped_node.as_str() && edge.to == candidate && edge.ramp. That avoided String versus unknown-type comparison errors.
